cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Regulatory capital applies to every risk-taking business, whereas risk capital applies only to closely supervised industries such as banking and insurance.
cards.explanation: Risk capital is the general concept that applies to any risk-taking business, whereas regulatory capital applies only to a few regulated industries such as banking and insurance.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Regulatory capital is derived from the firm's own characteristics and investment choices, whereas risk capital is derived from industry-wide rules and formulas.
cards.explanation: The sources are reversed: risk capital depends on firm-specific policy parameters set by senior management, while regulatory capital is computed under industry-wide rules and formulas.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Risk capital is calculated at a confidence level and time horizon that are the firm's own policy parameters, whereas regulatory capital follows industry-wide rules and establishes only a minimum level of capital adequacy.
cards.explanation: Risk capital's confidence level and horizon are policy parameters set by senior management and endorsed by the board, while regulatory capital is computed under industry-wide rules and sets only a minimum standard of capital adequacy.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: If aggregate risk capital and regulatory capital are close at the level of the firm, they will also be close for each constituent business line.
cards.explanation: Even when aggregate risk capital and regulatory capital are close at firm level, they can differ substantially for individual business lines, which is what makes allocating capital costs to business lines difficult.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Economic capital is smaller than risk capital, because risk capital is the amount required to guarantee stakeholders with 100% confidence that the firm holds enough capital to ride out any eventuality.
cards.explanation: Economic capital is never smaller than risk capital, since it equals risk capital plus strategic risk capital. No firm can offer a 100% confidence guarantee, so risk capital is set at a confidence level below 100%, such as 99.9%.
cards.originalText: "Economic capital is smaller than risk capital, because risk capital is the amount required to guarantee our stakeholders with 100% confidence that we hold enough capital to ride out any eventuality."

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: In a securitisation business regulatory capital is almost certainly higher than economic capital, so there is no reason to compute economic capital for that business at all.
cards.explanation: Basel III can push regulatory capital above economic capital for activities such as securitisation, but economic capital remains senior management's benchmark for economic viability. Where regulatory capital greatly exceeds economic capital, the activity tends to migrate to the shadow banking sector.
cards.originalText: "In our securitisation business regulatory capital is almost certainly higher than economic capital, so there is no reason for us to compute economic capital for that business at all."

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: A firm needs enough risk capital to absorb unexpected losses and remain solvent over a chosen time horizon at a chosen confidence level, and unlike regulatory capital that horizon and that confidence level are the firm's own policy parameters.
cards.explanation: Risk capital is the cushion that absorbs unexpected losses and keeps the firm solvent at a chosen confidence level over a chosen horizon, and those parameters are set by senior management and endorsed by the board rather than prescribed by regulators.
cards.originalText: "We need enough risk capital to absorb unexpected losses and remain solvent over a chosen time horizon at a chosen confidence level, and unlike regulatory capital that horizon and that confidence level are our own policy parameters."

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: For capital budgeting, ex ante RAROC should be used with economic capital in the numerator; for performance evaluation, ex post RAROC should be used with regulatory capital in the numerator.
cards.explanation: Capital sits in the denominator of RAROC, not the numerator, and it is economic capital in both ex ante and ex post uses. Regulatory capital does not enter RAROC.
cards.originalText: "For capital budgeting we should use ex ante RAROC with economic capital in the numerator; for performance evaluation we should use ex post RAROC with regulatory capital in the numerator."

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Expected loss is excluded from risk capital because it is a cost of doing business, provisioned for and priced into the transaction as a spread, so capital buffers only unexpected loss; lowering the confidence level reduces the amount of risk capital allocated to an activity.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is a cost of doing business that is provisioned and priced into the transaction as a spread, so risk capital buffers only unexpected loss. A lower confidence level captures less of the loss tail and so requires less capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Expected loss is excluded from risk capital because it is not a cost of doing business; lowering the confidence level increases the amount of risk capital allocated, because a wider portion of the loss distribution is captured.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is a cost of doing business priced in as a spread, which is why it is excluded from risk capital. A lower confidence level captures a narrower portion of the loss distribution and reduces risk capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Expected loss is included within risk capital because loan loss provisions may prove insufficient; the confidence level does not affect the amount of capital allocated, only the volatility of that amount from period to period.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is deducted in the RAROC numerator rather than buffered by capital. The confidence level directly affects the amount of capital; the volatility of economic capital over time is governed by the point-in-time versus through-the-cycle choice.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Expected loss is excluded from risk capital because it is fully diversifiable across a large portfolio; raising the confidence level to 100% would make risk capital equal to the total exposure.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is excluded from risk capital because it is a priced-in cost of doing business, not because it is diversifiable. A 100% confidence level is unattainable, since no firm can offer stakeholders that guarantee.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Risk capital numbers answer the solvency question first and are then extended to performance measurement and incentive compensation, to entry and exit decisions, and to risk-based pricing of individual transactions; a single measure of risk capital cannot accommodate all of these purposes.
cards.explanation: Risk capital is first used to establish how much capital keeps the firm solvent, and is then used for performance measurement and incentive compensation, entry and exit decisions, and risk-based pricing. Because these purposes differ, no single measure of risk capital can serve them all.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Capital in a financial institution is used primarily to fund investments, exactly as in a manufacturing corporation, which is why return on book equity remains an appropriate performance measure for both.
cards.explanation: Capital in a financial institution absorbs risk as well as funding investment, unlike in a manufacturing corporation. Accounting measures such as return on book equity fail to capture the risk of the underlying activity.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Because banks are transparent institutions whose balance sheets change only slowly, external stakeholders can assess creditworthiness directly, so economic capital serves mainly an internal reporting function.
cards.explanation: Banks are highly opaque and have relatively liquid balance sheets that can change very quickly, so outside assessments of their creditworthiness are hard to develop and quickly become obsolete.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Risk Capital, Economic Capital and Regulatory Capital: define, compare and contrast risk capital, economic capital and regulatory capital.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Because risk capital is cheaper to raise and hold than debt capital, banks should carry as much of it as regulators permit.
cards.explanation: Risk capital does not have to be repaid under any fixed contractual agreement, and that flexibility makes it relatively expensive to raise and hold compared with debt capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: RAROC risk-adjusts the numerator by subtracting a risk factor such as expected loss from the return, and risk-adjusts the denominator by substituting economic capital for accounting capital, so RAROC is ratio consistent.
cards.explanation: RAROC subtracts a risk factor such as expected loss from the return in the numerator and uses economic capital in the denominator, so both parts are risk-adjusted and the measure is ratio consistent.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: RORAC, also called ROC or ROCAR, adjusts only the denominator, in practical applications by placing VaR there. Because its numerator is net income, RORAC is ratio inconsistent.
cards.explanation: RORAC (also called ROC or ROCAR) risk-adjusts only the denominator, typically with VaR, while its numerator remains net income, so it is ratio inconsistent.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: RAROA and RORAA share the same denominator, risk-adjusted assets, but RAROA employs risk-adjusted expected net income in the numerator while RORAA employs net income, so RAROA is ratio consistent while RORAA is not.
cards.explanation: RAROA and RORAA both use risk-adjusted assets in the denominator. RAROA also risk-adjusts the numerator, making it ratio consistent, while RORAA uses unadjusted net income and is not.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: NPV is the discounted value of expected cash flows, but its glaring weakness is that it is not compatible with the capital asset pricing model and, relatedly, has no convenient method for incorporating risk.
cards.explanation: NPV discounts expected cash flows at a risk-adjusted rate of return based on the CAPM beta, so it is built on the CAPM and incorporates risk through the discount rate.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: NIACC is after-tax adjusted net income less a capital charge equal to the economic capital attributed to the activity multiplied by the after-tax cost of equity capital, and an activity whose RAROC exceeds the hurdle rate is necessarily EVA positive.
cards.explanation: NIACC equals after-tax adjusted net income minus economic capital times the after-tax cost of equity. Since the hurdle rate is the after-tax cost of equity, RAROC above the hurdle rate implies positive NIACC, meaning the activity is EVA positive.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: NIACC is after-tax adjusted net income less a capital charge equal to the regulatory capital attributed to the activity multiplied by the after-tax cost of debt, and an activity whose RAROC exceeds the risk-free rate is necessarily EVA positive.
cards.explanation: The NIACC capital charge is economic capital (not regulatory capital) times the after-tax cost of equity (not debt), and the RAROC benchmark for EVA positivity is the hurdle rate, not the risk-free rate.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: NIACC is computed before tax and therefore cannot be reconciled with RAROC, which is defined on an after-tax basis.
cards.explanation: NIACC is defined on after-tax adjusted net income with a capital charge at the after-tax cost of equity, so it is on the same after-tax basis as RAROC and the two reconcile exactly.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: An activity is EVA positive when its adjusted RAROC exceeds the firm's hurdle rate, which is precisely why the adjusted measure is preferred to the traditional one.
cards.explanation: The equivalence with EVA positivity links traditional RAROC to the hurdle rate. Adjusted RAROC is benchmarked against the risk-free rate.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: RAROC was first suggested as a tool for capital allocation on an anticipatory or ex ante basis, so expected revenues and expected losses belong in the numerator for capital budgeting; when RAROC is used ex post for performance evaluation, realised revenues and realised losses are used instead.
cards.explanation: Ex ante RAROC for capital budgeting uses expected revenues and expected losses in the numerator, while ex post RAROC for performance evaluation uses realised revenues and realised losses. Economic capital is the denominator in both.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Expected revenues and expected losses are used in both cases, because using realised figures for performance evaluation would make results incomparable across business units.
cards.explanation: Ex post performance evaluation uses realised revenues and losses. Using only forecasts would make it impossible to detect variances between what was projected and what actually occurred.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Realised revenues and realised losses are used in both cases, because capital budgeting decisions must be grounded in observed rather than forecast outcomes.
cards.explanation: Realised figures do not exist when a capital budgeting decision is taken, so ex ante RAROC uses expected revenues and losses to price and select deals in advance.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe the RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital) methodology and its use in capital budgeting.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: The numerator is identical in both cases; what changes is the denominator, with economic capital used ex ante and regulatory capital used ex post.
cards.explanation: It is the numerator inputs that change (expected versus realised revenues and losses), while economic capital is the denominator in both uses.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in using RAROC for performance measurement, including choosing a time horizon, choosing a basis for measuring default probabilities, and choosing a confidence level.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: When converting a trading desk's one-day VaR into one-year risk capital, it should be scaled by the square root of the number of business days and then scaled up further, because volatility clustering means the square root rule understates one-year risk.
cards.explanation: Naive square-root-of-time scaling overstates one-year market risk capital, because it ignores the fact that positions are run down to a core risk level during a crisis.
cards.originalText: Scale the one-day VaR by the square root of the number of business days and then scale it up further, because volatility clustering means the square root rule understates one-year risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in using RAROC for performance measurement, including choosing a time horizon, choosing a basis for measuring default probabilities, and choosing a confidence level.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: In a crisis a trading desk will run its position down over the time to reduce to a core risk level and hold it there for the remainder of the year, so that its one-year risk capital is well below annualised VaR.
cards.explanation: In a crisis a trading desk reduces its exposure over the time to reduce to a core risk level and holds it there for the rest of the year, so its one-year risk capital is well below naively annualised VaR.
cards.originalText: Recognise that in a crisis the desk will run its position down over the time to reduce to a core risk level and hold it there for the remainder of the year, so that risk capital is well below annualised VaR.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in using RAROC for performance measurement, including choosing a time horizon, choosing a basis for measuring default probabilities, and choosing a confidence level.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: One-year risk capital for a trading desk should assume the position is sold in a fire sale on the first day of a crisis, so that risk capital equals the one-day VaR.
cards.explanation: Estimates of the time to reduce should not assume a fire sale, and exposure falls to a core risk level rather than to zero, so one-year risk capital does not collapse to the one-day VaR.
cards.originalText: Assume the position is sold in a fire sale on the first day of the crisis, so that risk capital equals the one-day VaR.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Aggregate firm-wide risk capital should lie between the square root of the sum of the squared stand-alone risk capitals, which corresponds to zero correlation, and the simple sum of the stand-alone risk capitals, which corresponds to perfect correlation.
cards.explanation: Without a fully integrated model, aggregate risk capital is bounded below by the zero-correlation case (square root of the sum of squared stand-alone capitals) and above by the perfect-correlation case (simple sum of stand-alone capitals).
cards.originalText: The aggregate should lie between the square root of the sum of the squared stand-alone risk capitals, which corresponds to zero correlation, and the simple sum of the stand-alone risk capitals, which corresponds to perfect correlation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Aggregate firm-wide risk capital should lie between the largest single stand-alone risk capital, which corresponds to perfect negative correlation, and the simple sum of the stand-alone risk capitals.
cards.explanation: The floor for aggregate risk capital is the zero-correlation case, the square root of the sum of squared stand-alone capitals, not the largest single stand-alone capital.
cards.originalText: The aggregate should lie between the largest single stand-alone risk capital, which corresponds to perfect negative correlation, and the simple sum of the stand-alone risk capitals.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Aggregate firm-wide risk capital should lie between zero, which corresponds to perfect negative correlation across all risk types simultaneously, and the simple sum of the stand-alone risk capitals.
cards.explanation: Perfect negative correlation across three or more positive risks at once is not attainable. The floor for aggregate risk capital is the zero-correlation case, the square root of the sum of squared stand-alone capitals.
cards.originalText: The aggregate should lie between zero, which corresponds to perfect negative correlation across all risk types simultaneously, and the simple sum of the stand-alone risk capitals.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Aggregate firm-wide risk capital should lie between the simple sum of the stand-alone risk capitals, which is the lower bound, and the square root of the sum of their squares, which is the upper bound.
cards.explanation: The bounds are reversed: the simple sum of stand-alone capitals (perfect correlation) is the maximum, and the square root of the sum of squares (zero correlation) is the minimum.
cards.originalText: The aggregate should lie between the simple sum of the stand-alone risk capitals, which is the lower bound, and the square root of the sum of their squares, which is the upper bound.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Fully diversified capital should be used for assessing the solvency of the firm and for minimum risk pricing.
cards.explanation: Fully diversified risk capital measures are the ones used for assessing firm solvency and for minimum risk pricing.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Marginal capital should be used for active portfolio management and business mix decisions.
cards.explanation: Active portfolio management and business mix decisions are based on marginal risk capital, which takes full account of diversification benefits.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Performance measurement should involve both perspectives: stand-alone capital for incentive compensation, and fully diversified capital to assess the extra performance generated by diversification effects.
cards.explanation: Performance measurement uses both perspectives: stand-alone capital for incentive compensation, and fully diversified capital to assess the extra performance generated by diversification.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Under a pro rata allocation, the fully diversified capitals of business units sum exactly to their combined risk capital, whereas the sum of their marginal capitals falls short of it.
cards.explanation: Because the whole portfolio effect is distributed under a pro rata allocation, fully diversified capitals reconcile exactly to the combined risk capital. Marginal capitals are not additive and sum to less than the combined figure.
cards.originalText: Under a pro rata allocation, the fully diversified capitals of the two departments sum exactly to the combined risk capital of the pair, whereas the sum of their marginal capitals would fall short of it.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Under a pro rata allocation, the fully diversified capitals of business units sum to the sum of their stand-alone capitals, so no capital is in fact released to any unit.
cards.explanation: Fully diversified capitals sum to the combined risk capital, which is smaller than the sum of stand-alone capitals, so the diversification benefit is released to the units in proportion to their stand-alone capital.
cards.originalText: Under a pro rata allocation, the fully diversified capitals sum to the sum of the stand-alone capitals, so no capital is in fact released to either department.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain the challenges in modelling diversification benefits, including the choice of a risk aggregation methodology and pricing considerations.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Pro rata allocation of the portfolio effect is theoretically preferred to alternatives because correlations between business lines are stable through time, which makes the allocated benefit reliable.
cards.explanation: Correlations between business lines vary over time and can shift dramatically in a crisis. Pro rata allocation is a practical convention adopted in the absence of an agreed theory, not a theoretically preferred method.
cards.originalText: The pro rata allocation is theoretically preferred to alternatives because correlations between business lines are stable through time, which makes the allocated benefit reliable.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain best practices in implementing an approach that ties economic capital to performance measurement.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Given the strategic nature of the decisions steered by a RAROC system, the marching orders must come from the top management of the firm; specifically the CEO and the executive team should sponsor the implementation and be active in its diffusion.
cards.explanation: Senior management commitment is the first best-practice recommendation for RAROC: because the system steers strategic decisions, the CEO and executive team should sponsor its implementation and actively promote it.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain best practices in implementing an approach that ties economic capital to performance measurement.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: In order to preserve the integrity and transparency of the RAROC system there should be an exclusively quantitative decision rule for activities: if the ex ante RAROC does not exceed the firm's hurdle rate, the firm should exit the activity.
cards.explanation: Best practice combines RAROC with qualitative factors, for example by assessing business units on a strategic grid, rather than relying on an exclusively quantitative accept-or-exit rule.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain best practices in implementing an approach that ties economic capital to performance measurement.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: The VaR methodologies for measuring market risk and credit risk that underpin RAROC calculations are generally well accepted by business units, although this is not yet true for operational risk; in practice disagreements concern the setting of the parameters that feed into these models and determine the size of economic capital.
cards.explanation: Business units generally accept VaR methodologies for market and credit risk, though not yet for operational risk. Disputes tend to concern the parameters that feed the models and determine the size of economic capital.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain best practices in implementing an approach that ties economic capital to performance measurement.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
cards.statement: Balance sheet requests from the business units, such as economic capital, leverage ratio, liquidity ratios and risk-weighted assets, should be channelled to the RAROC group every quarter, and limits are then set for each of these.
cards.explanation: Active capital management is a RAROC best practice: business units submit quarterly balance sheet requests (economic capital, leverage ratio, liquidity ratios and risk-weighted assets) to the RAROC group, which then sets limits for each.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain Basel regulatory expectations for the governance of an operational risk management framework.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Operational risk is the only risk type for which management principles are included in the Pillar 1 regulation, reflecting the regulatory view that no amount of capital can cover losses from operational failures in the absence of sound management.
cards.explanation: Regulators recognised from the start that no amount of capital may cover losses from operational failures without sound management, so Pillar 1 for operational risk includes mandatory management principles, uniquely among risk types.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain Basel regulatory expectations for the governance of an operational risk management framework.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Management principles for credit, market and operational risk are all included in Pillar 1, but only the operational risk principles are mandatory rather than advisory.
cards.explanation: Credit and market risk are addressed in Pillar 1 through capital calculation only. Operational risk is the only risk type whose management principles are included in Pillar 1.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain Basel regulatory expectations for the governance of an operational risk management framework.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The operational risk management principles sit in Pillar 2 rather than Pillar 1, because they are qualitative and Pillar 1 is restricted to quantitative capital calculations.
cards.explanation: The operational risk management principles sit in Pillar 1, not Pillar 2. Pillar 1 is not restricted to quantitative capital calculations.
cards.originalText: The management principles sit in Pillar 2 rather than Pillar 1, because they are qualitative and Pillar 1 is restricted to quantitative capital calculations.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Explain Basel regulatory expectations for the governance of an operational risk management framework.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The operational risk management principles sit in Pillar 3, because their primary purpose is to inform the market about the quality of a bank's operational risk management.
cards.explanation: Pillar 3 governs disclosure. Although one principle requires public disclosure of the approach to operational risk management, the principles as a body sit in Pillar 1.
cards.originalText: The management principles sit in Pillar 3, because their primary purpose is to inform the market about the quality of a bank's operational risk management.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The group operational risk committee oversees, manages, monitors and reports the consolidated operational risk picture to the executive risk committee, the management committee and the board risk committee.
cards.explanation: In a pyramid of operational risk committees, the group operational risk committee sits in the middle tier: it consolidates the operational risk picture and reports it upward to the executive risk committee, the management committee and the board risk committee.
cards.originalText: Overseeing, managing, monitoring and reporting the consolidated operational risk picture to the executive risk committee, the management committee and the board risk committee.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The group operational risk committee oversees operational risk within a single business line, function or geographic location.
cards.explanation: Oversight within a single business line, function or geography is the role of the lowest-tier committees. The group operational risk committee consolidates the firm-wide picture and reports it upward.
cards.originalText: Overseeing operational risk within a single business line, function or geographic location.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The group operational risk committee oversees all operational risk on behalf of the enterprise.
cards.explanation: Enterprise-wide oversight of all operational risk belongs to the board-created enterprise-level risk committee. The group operational risk committee consolidates and reports the operational risk picture to that committee and to executive bodies.
cards.originalText: Overseeing all operational risk on behalf of the enterprise.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Establishing and maintaining robust challenge mechanisms and effective issue-resolution processes is a responsibility of senior management.
cards.explanation: Building and running challenge mechanisms and issue-resolution processes is implementation work, which falls to senior management rather than the board.
cards.originalText: Establishing and maintaining robust challenge mechanisms and effective issue-resolution processes.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Translating the ORMF into specific policies and procedures that can be implemented and verified within the different business units is a responsibility of senior management.
cards.explanation: Under Principle 5 of the PSMOR, senior management translates the operational risk management framework into specific policies and procedures that can be implemented and verified within business units.
cards.originalText: Translating the ORMF into specific policies and procedures that can be implemented and verified within the different business units.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Recruiting experienced technical staff and ensuring a sufficient level of operational risk training in order to secure implementation of the ORMF is a responsibility of senior management.
cards.explanation: Recruiting staff and delivering operational risk training are resourcing decisions made by senior management to secure implementation of the framework.
cards.originalText: Recruiting experienced technical staff and ensuring a sufficient level of operational risk training in order to secure implementation of the ORMF.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Reviewing and approving the ORMF at regular intervals, to ensure that the bank is identifying and managing the operational risks arising from external market changes and other environmental factors, is a responsibility of the board of directors.
cards.explanation: Under Principle 3 of the PSMOR, the board reviews and approves the operational risk management framework at regular intervals and obtains assurance that senior management implements it effectively.
cards.originalText: Reviewing and approving the ORMF at regular intervals, to ensure that the bank is identifying and managing the operational risks arising from external market changes and other environmental factors.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Under the PSMOR, identifying the types and levels of operational risk the bank is willing to assume, and approving risk appetite and risk tolerance statements, is a board responsibility under Principle 4.
cards.explanation: Principle 4 covers the risk appetite and tolerance statement: the board identifies the types and levels of operational risk the bank is willing to assume and approves the appetite and tolerance statements.
cards.originalText: Identifying the types and levels of operational risk the bank is willing to assume, and approving risk appetite and risk tolerance statements.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the roles of committees and the board in operational risk governance.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Under the PSMOR, ensuring that the ORMF is subject to effective independent review by appropriately trained and skilled personnel is a board responsibility under Principle 3.
cards.explanation: Principle 3 requires the board to approve and periodically review the operational risk management framework, ensure it is subject to effective independent review, and obtain assurance that senior management implements it effectively.
cards.originalText: Ensuring that the ORMF is subject to effective independent review by appropriately trained and skilled personnel.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The first line of defence defines the organisation's risk appetite but should not attempt to influence its risk culture directly.
cards.explanation: The board defines risk appetite, and the first line operates within it. The first line is central to shaping the firm's risk culture rather than being excluded from it.
cards.originalText: The first line defines the organisation's risk appetite but should not attempt to influence its risk culture directly.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The first line of defence is responsible for implementing and maintaining effective controls to manage material operational risks.
cards.explanation: The first line of defence owns the risks where they are generated and is responsible for implementing and maintaining effective controls over material operational risks.
cards.originalText: The first line is responsible for implementing and maintaining effective controls to manage material operational risks.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The second line of defence is part of management and owns the operational risk methodology, but provides support to the first line in order to help the firm create and protect value.
cards.explanation: Under the IIA's 2021 Three Lines Model, the second line is part of management, not a quasi-audit function: it owns the operational risk methodology and supports the first line in creating and protecting value.
cards.originalText: The second line is part of management and owns the operational risk methodology, but provides support to the first line in order to help the firm create and protect value.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The third line has the clearest boundaries of the three, because of its independence.
cards.explanation: Because internal audit is independent of both management lines, the third line has the clearest boundaries of the three.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Monitoring and reporting the business units' operational risk profiles is a responsibility of the first line of defence.
cards.explanation: First-line responsibilities include identifying and assessing operational risks, establishing controls, assessing the design and effectiveness of those controls, and monitoring and reporting the business units' operational risk profiles.
cards.originalText: Monitoring and reporting the business units' operational risk profiles.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Developing and maintaining operational risk management and measurement policies, standards and guidelines, and designing and delivering operational risk training, is a responsibility of the first line of defence.
cards.explanation: Developing operational risk policies, standards and guidelines, and designing and delivering operational risk training, are responsibilities of the second line of defence.
cards.originalText: Developing and maintaining operational risk management and measurement policies, standards and guidelines, and designing and delivering operational risk training.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Providing independent assurance on the adequacy of the risk management function itself is a responsibility of the first line of defence.
cards.explanation: Independent assurance, including over the risk management function itself, is provided by the third line of defence, internal audit.
cards.originalText: Providing independent assurance on the adequacy of the risk management function itself.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: To maintain independence, an operational risk management framework prohibits any reporting relationship, even a dotted line, from the CORF to either the Chief Risk Officer or the board's risk committee.
cards.explanation: The CORF must be independent of the risk-generating business units. A reporting line to the Chief Risk Officer and on to the board risk committee is what delivers that independence.
cards.originalText: To maintain independence, the framework prohibits any reporting relationship, even a dotted line, from the CORF to either the Chief Risk Officer or the board's risk committee.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: An operational risk management framework should provide a common taxonomy of operational risk terms to ensure consistency of risk identification, exposure rating and risk management objectives.
cards.explanation: A common operational risk taxonomy, including loss event types, is required so that risks are identified, rated and managed consistently across the firm.
cards.originalText: The framework should provide a common taxonomy of operational risk terms to ensure consistency of risk identification, exposure rating and risk management objectives.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Compensation plans should be aligned with the bank's risk appetite and risk tolerance, and may include incentive compensation explicitly linked to risk-adjusted measures, deferral mechanisms or claw-backs.
cards.explanation: Compensation is tied to risk culture and to the principle that risk-takers should bear the consequences of their actions, through tools such as risk-adjusted incentives, deferrals and claw-backs.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The board approves a risk appetite statement, a forward-looking high-level view of risk acceptance incorporating return expectations, and a risk tolerance statement, a more specific determination of the level of variation the bank is willing to accept around business objectives.
cards.explanation: The board approves both statements. Risk appetite is the broader, forward-looking view of risk acceptance, while risk tolerance specifies the acceptable variation around business objectives.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Business line management is not a line of defence.
cards.explanation: Business line management is the first line of defence, which BCBS describes as business unit management.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The independent review of an operational risk management framework includes neither verification nor validation.
cards.explanation: The independent review of an operational risk management framework includes both verification and validation.
cards.originalText: Independent review includes neither verification nor validation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Auditors performing the independent review of an operational risk management framework cannot be involved in the framework's design, development or implementation.
cards.explanation: Auditors who design or implement the framework would lose the independence that gives their assurance value, so they must not be involved in its design, development or implementation.
cards.originalText: The auditors cannot be involved in the framework's design, development or implementation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The independent review of an operational risk management framework cannot be conducted internally and must be performed by external parties.
cards.explanation: The independent review may be conducted by internal or external audit. What matters is independence from those who built the framework, not whether the reviewer is inside or outside the firm.
cards.originalText: The independent review cannot be conducted internally and must be performed by external parties.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: In applying the three lines of defence model, each department must be assigned in its entirety to a single line of defence, because a department cannot belong to two lines at once.
cards.explanation: Departments may span two lines of defence. What defines a line is the roles and responsibilities attributed to a department rather than its name, so hybrid functions should document and distinguish their first and second line responsibilities.
cards.originalText: Each department must be assigned in its entirety to a single line of defence, because a department cannot belong to two lines at once.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: The responsibilities of functions that perform both first and second line activities should be documented and distinguished, emphasising the independence of the second line, because what defines a line is the roles and responsibilities attributed to a department rather than its name.
cards.explanation: What defines a line of defence is the roles and responsibilities attributed to a department, not its name. Where resource-constrained functions perform both first and second line activities, those responsibilities should be documented and distinguished, with emphasis on second-line independence.
cards.originalText: The responsibilities of such functions in the first and second line should be documented and distinguished, emphasising the independence of the second line, because what defines a line is the roles and responsibilities attributed to a department rather than its name.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: In the three lines of defence model, hybrid functions are permitted only where the corporate operational risk function has a reporting structure independent of the risk-generating business units, which is achievable only at large banks.
cards.explanation: Hybrid functions are most common at smaller institutions. Independent CORF reporting lines are expected at larger banks, while at small banks independence can be achieved through separation of duties and independent review.
cards.originalText: Hybrid functions are permitted only where the corporate operational risk function has a reporting structure independent of the risk-generating business units, which is achievable only at large banks.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Describe and compare the three lines of defence model.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 2: Risk Governance
cards.statement: Control functions such as legal, finance and IT security fall outside the three lines of defence model entirely, since the model applies only to revenue-generating business lines and to the risk and audit functions.
cards.explanation: Control functions are inside the three lines model; their difficulty is that they can straddle lines. The corporate operational risk function typically engages compliance, legal, finance and IT to support its assessment of operational risks and controls.
cards.originalText: Control functions such as legal, finance and IT security fall outside the three lines model entirely, since the model applies only to revenue-generating business lines and to the risk and audit functions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: The FSB Cyber Lexicon definition of cyber-resilience includes anticipating and adapting to cyber threats and other relevant changes in the environment.
cards.explanation: The FSB Cyber Lexicon defines cyber-resilience as the ability to continue carrying out the organisation's mission by anticipating and adapting to cyber threats and other relevant changes in the environment, and by withstanding, containing and rapidly recovering from cyber incidents.
cards.originalText: Anticipating and adapting to cyber threats and other relevant changes in the environment

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: The FSB Cyber Lexicon definition of cyber-resilience includes withstanding and containing cyber incidents.
cards.explanation: The FSB Cyber Lexicon defines cyber-resilience as the ability to continue carrying out the organisation's mission by anticipating and adapting to cyber threats and other relevant changes in the environment, and by withstanding, containing and rapidly recovering from cyber incidents.
cards.originalText: Withstanding and containing cyber incidents

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: The FSB Cyber Lexicon definition of cyber-resilience includes rapidly recovering from cyber incidents.
cards.explanation: The FSB Cyber Lexicon defines cyber-resilience as the ability to continue carrying out the organisation's mission by anticipating and adapting to cyber threats and other relevant changes in the environment, and by withstanding, containing and rapidly recovering from cyber incidents.
cards.originalText: Rapidly recovering from cyber incidents

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: A bank's cyber-security approach should aim to identify every cyber vulnerability capable of exposing it to large-scale monetary or non-monetary loss, with a view to the complete eradication of those threats.
cards.explanation: Completely eradicating cyber threats is unattainable given a growing attack surface and adaptive adversaries. The goal is to reduce threat and build resilience.
cards.originalText: Identify every cyber vulnerability capable of exposing the bank to large-scale monetary or non-monetary loss, with a view to the complete eradication of those threats.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: Absolute cyber security is unattainable, so banks should instead build a robust IT capability together with local and international cooperation and information exchange, in order to reduce threat and build resilience.
cards.explanation: Absolute security is unattainable, so the Basel Committee's range of practices report points to robust IT capability combined with local and international cooperation and information exchange as the way to reduce threat and build resilience.
cards.originalText: Accept that absolute security is unattainable, and instead build a robust IT capability together with local and international cooperation and information exchange, in order to reduce threat and build resilience.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: Banks should reduce their use of third-party providers and cloud services, since these are what have caused the attack surface to grow and become shared.
cards.explanation: Third parties and cloud services have indeed enlarged the attack surface and made it shared, but the prescribed response is to build resilience in partnership with third parties, supported by mapping, contractual protections, audit rights and aligned continuity plans.
cards.originalText: Reduce the bank's use of third-party providers and cloud services, since these are what have caused the attack surface to grow and become shared.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: All regulators expect regulated entities to have a board-approved information security strategy, policy and procedures.
cards.explanation: Although most regulators do not require a standalone cyber-security strategy, all expect regulated institutions to have a board-approved information security strategy, policy and procedures.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: Most jurisdictions expect cyber-risk to be covered by the organisation-wide risk management framework or information security framework.
cards.explanation: Most jurisdictions expect cyber-risk to be covered by the organisation-wide risk management framework or the information security framework.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: Most supervisors review regulated entities' information security strategies, but very few require or evaluate a standalone cyber-security strategy.
cards.explanation: Supervisors generally review information security strategies, but very few require or evaluate a standalone cyber-security strategy.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: In most jurisdictions the development of a standalone cyber-security strategy is a mandatory requirement anchored in law.
cards.explanation: Most regulators do not require regulated entities to develop a standalone cyber-security strategy. What is universally expected is a board-approved information security strategy, policy and procedures.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: Responsibility for an outsourced activity transfers to the service provider once the contract is signed, so a cloud provider falls outside the outsourcing firm's cyber-risk framework.
cards.explanation: Ultimate responsibility for an outsourced activity remains with the outsourcing institution, and cloud providers fall within the perimeter of supervisory interest.
cards.originalText: Treat the cloud provider as outside the scope of the firm's framework, since responsibility for the outsourced activity transfers to the provider once the contract is signed.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: In the Basel Committee's range of practices report, sharing among regulators is the least observed of the five types of cyber-security information sharing, and jurisdictions with well-established sharing among banks tend to show fewer observed practices of sharing from regulators to banks.
cards.explanation: Sharing among regulators is the least observed type, at about 29% of jurisdictions. Jurisdictions where sharing among banks is well established tend to show fewer practices of sharing from regulators to banks.
cards.originalText: Sharing among regulators is the least observed of the five types, and jurisdictions with well-established sharing among banks tend to show fewer observed practices of sharing from regulators to banks.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: Sharing from regulators to banks is the most widely observed type of cyber-security information sharing, because regulators hold the most complete threat picture.
cards.explanation: Sharing from regulators to banks is the second-least observed type (about 32% of jurisdictions). Sharing among banks and from banks to regulators are the most commonly observed.
cards.originalText: Sharing from regulators to banks is the most widely observed type, because regulators hold the most complete threat picture.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: Sharing among banks is the least observed type of cyber-security information sharing, since competitive concerns prevent peer institutions from disclosing threat intelligence.
cards.explanation: Sharing among banks is joint-most observed (about 75% of jurisdictions), and cyber-threat intelligence is the most common kind of information shared through that channel.
cards.originalText: Sharing among banks is the least observed type, since competitive concerns prevent peer institutions from disclosing threat intelligence.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 8: Cyber-Resilience: Range of Practices (BCBS)
cards.statement: Full adoption of all five types of cyber-security information-sharing arrangement within a jurisdiction is now the norm rather than the exception.
cards.explanation: The Basel Committee's range of practices report states that having all types of cyber-security information-sharing arrangements in place within a jurisdiction is still exceptional.
cards.originalText: Full adoption of all five types of information-sharing arrangement within a jurisdiction is now the norm rather than the exception.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: Virus infection is an example of loss or involuntary disclosure from an external cause.
cards.explanation: Virus infection is a deliberate external act, classed as theft or corruption alongside hacking and phishing, not as loss or involuntary disclosure.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: Systems disruptions and third-party failure are examples of loss or involuntary disclosure from an external cause.
cards.explanation: External causes of loss or involuntary disclosure include disasters, systems disruptions and third-party failure.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: A departing employee taking proprietary information is an example of theft or corruption from an external cause.
cards.explanation: A departing employee taking proprietary information is theft or corruption from an internal cause, a mishandled exit.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: Loss of printed documents is an example of theft or corruption from an internal cause.
cards.explanation: Loss of printed documents is involuntary, so it is loss or involuntary disclosure from an internal cause, not theft or corruption.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: In the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the Identify function includes making a list of all equipment, software and data in use, and creating and sharing a company cybersecurity policy covering roles and responsibilities for employees, vendors and anyone else with access to sensitive data.
cards.explanation: Under NIST's Identify function, the firm inventories its equipment, software and data and creates a cybersecurity policy setting out roles and responsibilities. The policy sits under Identify, not Protect.
cards.originalText: Identify: make a list of all equipment, software and data in use, and create and share a company cybersecurity policy covering roles and responsibilities for employees, vendors and anyone else with access to sensitive data.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: In the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the Protect function includes controlling who logs on to the network, encrypting sensitive data at rest and in transit, conducting regular back-ups, updating security software, and training everyone who uses the firm's computers and network.
cards.explanation: NIST's Protect function covers access control, encryption, back-ups, security software updates and training users. Training sits under Protect while the cybersecurity policy sits under Identify.
cards.originalText: Protect: control who logs on to the network, encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit, conduct regular back-ups, update security software, and train everyone who uses the firm's computers and network.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: In the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the Detect function includes creating and regularly testing a plan for notifying customers and employees whose data may be at risk and for reporting the attack to law enforcement and other authorities.
cards.explanation: Planning how to notify affected customers and employees and how to report an attack to law enforcement and other authorities belongs to the Respond function of the NIST framework, not Detect.
cards.originalText: Detect: create and regularly test a plan for notifying customers and employees whose data may be at risk and for reporting the attack to law enforcement and other authorities.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: In the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the Recover function includes repairing and restoring the equipment and parts of the network affected, and keeping employees and customers informed of response and recovery activities.
cards.explanation: NIST's Recover function covers repairing and restoring affected equipment and network parts and keeping employees and customers informed of response and recovery activities.
cards.originalText: Recover: repair and restore the equipment and parts of the network affected, and keep employees and customers informed of response and recovery activities.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: ISO/IEC 27001 certification requires an organisation to operate an Information Security Management System that systematically manages the organisation's information security risks by identifying threats and vulnerabilities.
cards.explanation: The Information Security Management System, which systematically identifies threats and vulnerabilities and manages information security risks, is the central requirement for ISO/IEC 27001 certification.
cards.originalText: Operate an Information Security Management System that systematically manages the organisation's information security risks by identifying threats and vulnerabilities.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
cards.statement: ISO/IEC 27001 certification requires an organisation to design and implement information security, including effective and comprehensive controls to mitigate the risks identified.
cards.explanation: ISO/IEC 27001 certification requires the organisation to design and implement information security, including effective and comprehensive controls over identified risks.
cards.originalText: Design and implement information security, including effective and comprehensive controls to mitigate the risks identified.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of and describe cyber threats, information security risks, and frameworks for managing them.
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 9: Case Study: Cyberthreats and Information Security Risks
