cards.explanation: Past performance does not control future capability, and a provider's risk profile changes over time, so incumbent providers remain subject to risk-based due diligence and monitoring.
cards.originalText: Perform due diligence only on newly appointed providers, since incumbent providers have demonstrated their capability through performance.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A contract for a material outsourced activity should address scope and performance standards with measurable service levels; reporting and monitoring rights; the right to audit and access records; confidentiality, data security and data ownership; business continuity and disaster recovery obligations; subcontracting; indemnification and limitation of liability; insurance; dispute resolution; and default, termination rights and transition assistance on exit.
cards.explanation: An outsourcing contract cannot transfer responsibility, but it turns supervisory expectations into enforceable obligations, securing the information, access and remedies the institution needs to discharge its accountability.
cards.originalText: Scope of the arrangement and performance standards with measurable service levels; reporting and monitoring rights; the right to audit and access records; confidentiality, data security and data ownership; business continuity and disaster recovery obligations; subcontracting; indemnification and limitation of liability; insurance; dispute resolution; default, termination rights and transition assistance on exit.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A contract for a material outsourced activity should address scope, price and term only, since operational matters are better handled through the service relationship than through legal drafting.
cards.explanation: A service relationship is worth little once it deteriorates, which is exactly when the contract is needed. Outsourcing contracts must address operational matters such as audit rights, data security, continuity and exit.
cards.originalText: Scope, price and term only, since operational matters are better handled through the service relationship than through legal drafting.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A contract for a material outsourced activity need only address scope, price and a general obligation on the provider to comply with all applicable laws, since this captures every regulatory requirement without needing enumeration.
cards.explanation: A general compliance covenant provides no audit rights, data provisions, continuity obligations or exit mechanism, and nothing specific to enforce.
cards.originalText: Scope, price and a general obligation on the provider to comply with all applicable laws, which is sufficient because it captures every regulatory requirement without needing enumeration.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A contract for a material outsourced activity should deliberately omit audit and data provisions so as not to deter competitive providers from bidding.
cards.explanation: Audit and data provisions are supervisory expectations, not negotiable extras. A provider unwilling to grant them should not be selected.
cards.originalText: Scope, performance standards and termination rights, with audit and data provisions deliberately omitted so as not to deter competitive providers from bidding.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A service provider's incentive compensation arrangements are a matter for the provider's own human resources policy and fall outside the scope of the outsourcing bank's risk management programme.
cards.explanation: Incentive compensation review is an express element of the service provider risk management programme, because the provider's pay design drives conduct towards the bank's customers.
cards.originalText: The compensation arrangement is a matter for the provider's own human resources policy and falls outside the scope of the bank's programme.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A bank should review an outsourced service provider's incentive compensation arrangements to determine whether they encourage imprudent risk taking or conduct that is inconsistent with the bank's own standards, and should address the matter contractually where they do.
cards.explanation: The provider's staff deal with the bank's customers in the bank's name, so conduct risk from their pay design lands on the bank. Incentive compensation review is a named element of the service provider programme.
cards.originalText: The bank should review the provider's incentive compensation arrangements to determine whether they encourage imprudent risk taking or conduct that is inconsistent with the bank's own standards, and should address the matter contractually where they do.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A bank should require an outsourced service provider to abolish variable compensation entirely, since any performance-linked pay creates conduct risk.
cards.explanation: The requirement is to review provider incentives and address problems, not to prohibit variable pay. Variable pay balanced with quality and compliance metrics can be consistent with good conduct.
cards.originalText: The bank should require the provider to abolish variable compensation entirely, since any performance-linked pay creates conduct risk.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: For a critical outsourced service, a contractual termination right is sufficient protection, since the firm can exit any relationship that fails.
cards.explanation: A right the firm cannot practically exercise is not protection. For a critical service, exit requires transition assistance, portable data, an alternative provider or in-house capability, and adequate notice.
cards.originalText: The termination right is sufficient protection, since the bank can exit any relationship that fails.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A termination right is of limited value for a critical service unless it is accompanied by transition assistance obligations, data return in a usable format, a realistic exit plan identifying an alternative provider or in-house capability, and a notice period long enough for that transition to occur.
cards.explanation: For a critical service the constraint on exit is operational rather than legal. Without somewhere else to run the service, portable data and the provider's cooperation during migration, exercising a termination right turns a service problem into an outage.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Contract topics and provisions. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: Termination rights are unnecessary where business continuity provisions are in place, since continuity obligations ensure the service will not fail.
cards.explanation: Business continuity provisions address disruption within a continuing relationship. They do not help when the firm needs to leave the provider for performance, conduct, financial or strategic reasons.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the third-party case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: A firm may outsource an activity but not the accountability for it, so the firm's exposure becomes a dependency on someone else's control environment, and the monitoring must reach the controls it now depends on rather than stopping at the contract.
cards.explanation: Across the third-party case studies, the firm remains accountable after outsourcing, so its risk becomes a dependency on the provider's controls. Monitoring must therefore extend to those controls, not stop at the contract.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the third-party case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: Third-party incidents arise principally from provider insolvency, so financial monitoring of providers is the highest-value control.
cards.explanation: The third-party cases turn on operational, security and conduct failures at solvent providers. Financial monitoring is necessary but is not where the losses came from.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the third-party case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: Firms that contract only with large, well-established providers do not experience material third-party incidents.
cards.explanation: The third-party case studies involve substantial, well-established providers, so provider size offers no guarantee against material incidents.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the third-party case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: Where a provider is itself regulated, the institution may rely on the provider's supervisor and reduce its own oversight accordingly.
cards.explanation: A provider being regulated does not allow the institution to reduce its own oversight. Relying on the provider's supervisor is identified as a specific hazard.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the third-party case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: Requiring a service provider to self-report all control failures removes the need for the outsourcing bank's own monitoring.
cards.explanation: Provider self-reporting is a valuable input but cannot replace the institution's own monitoring, for the same reason self-certification cannot test itself.
cards.originalText: The bank should have required the provider to self-report all control failures, which would have removed the need for the bank's own monitoring.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the third-party case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: Customer complaints are the appropriate primary detection mechanism for third-party failures, since customers experience the service directly.
cards.explanation: Complaints are a lagging indicator: by the time customers complain, harm has already occurred. They confirm failures but should not be the primary detection mechanism.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from investor protection and compliance cases. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: The dominant investor protection failure is mis-selling, arising where the product, the client and the incentive are misaligned, and the losses are driven less by the individual transaction than by the systematic repetition of the same defective process across a large customer base.
cards.explanation: Investor protection failures are process failures repeated at scale: a product, client and incentive that are misaligned, applied to many customers over years, as in the payment protection insurance episode.
cards.originalText: The dominant failure is mis-selling, arising where the product, the client and the incentive are misaligned, and the losses are driven less by the individual transaction than by the systematic repetition of the same defective process across a large customer base.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from investor protection and compliance cases. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: The dominant investor protection failure is fraud by individual advisers acting outside firm policy, which is best addressed through enhanced background screening.
cards.explanation: Investor protection cases typically involve approved products sold through approved processes to the wrong customers, not rogue advisers acting outside firm policy.
cards.originalText: The dominant failure is fraud by individual advisers acting outside firm policy, which is best addressed through enhanced background screening.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from investor protection and compliance cases. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: In investor protection cases, the losses are principally market losses suffered by clients, for which the firm is held liable under a strict liability standard.
cards.explanation: Firms are not liable for clients' market losses as such. Liability arises from failures in the sales and advice process, so a client who lost money on a suitable, properly explained product has no claim.
cards.originalText: The losses in these cases were principally market losses suffered by clients, for which the firm was held liable under a strict liability standard.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from investor protection and compliance cases. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: The cases show that investor protection breaches are typically detected and remediated by firms themselves before regulatory involvement.
cards.explanation: Investor protection breaches typically persist for years, are often surfaced by complaints, regulatory thematic reviews or press attention, and are remediated under supervisory pressure.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from investor protection and compliance cases. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk (Federal Reserve)
cards.statement: To prevent recurrence of mis-selling, a firm should establish product governance with a documented target market and distribution strategy, align suitability assessment to that target market, remove or rebalance incentives that reward volume irrespective of suitability, and monitor complaint and outcome data by product and by distributor as a leading indicator.
cards.explanation: Because mis-selling is a systematic process failure, the controls must be systematic: product governance, suitability aligned to the target market, incentives that do not reward volume regardless of suitability, and outcome monitoring as a leading indicator.
cards.originalText: Establish product governance with a documented target market and distribution strategy, align suitability assessment to that target market, remove or rebalance incentives that reward volume irrespective of suitability, and monitor complaint and outcome data by product and by distributor as a leading indicator.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model development should begin from a clear statement of purpose that aligns the model with its intended use; the quality and relevance of the data should be assessed and documented; the merits and limitations of the chosen methodology and its processing components should be explained; and the model should be compared against alternative approaches and theories.
cards.explanation: Model developers must set out a clear statement of purpose, assess and document data quality and relevance, explain the methodology's merits and limitations, and compare the model with alternative approaches before handing it to validation.
cards.originalText: Development should begin from a clear statement of purpose that aligns the model with its intended use; the quality and relevance of the data should be assessed and documented; the merits and limitations of the chosen methodology and its processing components should be explained; and the model should be compared against alternative approaches and theories.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model development should begin from the data available, with the purpose defined afterwards to fit whatever the data can support.
cards.explanation: Model development starts with a clear statement of purpose aligned to intended use, because purpose defines what a correct model is. Data-led development produces a model that addresses whatever the data happens to support rather than what the business needs.
cards.originalText: Development should begin from the data available, with the purpose defined afterwards to fit whatever the data can support.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: In model development, comparison against alternative approaches belongs exclusively to validation and should be avoided by developers, since it would compromise their objectivity.
cards.explanation: Comparing the model with alternative approaches is an express developer obligation as well as a validation activity. Objectivity is secured by independent validation.
cards.originalText: Comparison against alternative approaches belongs exclusively to validation and should be avoided by developers, since it would compromise their objectivity.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Documentation of a model's limitations should be deferred until validation, since recording weaknesses during development would prejudice the model's approval.
cards.explanation: Developers are expected to explain and document a model's limitations during development. Documentation exists so that users and validators understand where the model does not work.
cards.originalText: Documentation of limitations should be deferred until validation, since recording weaknesses during development would prejudice the model's approval.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: When a validated model is deployed into production, the key practices are systems implementation testing including code verification and user acceptance testing, controls over the production environment and change management, and a clear communication to users of the model's intended scope and its documented limitations.
cards.explanation: Implementation can create model risk even for a conceptually sound model. Code verification and user testing, change control over the production environment, and clear communication of scope and limitations address that risk.
cards.originalText: Systems implementation testing including code verification and user acceptance testing, controls over the production environment and change management, and a clear communication to users of the model's intended scope and its documented limitations.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: When a validated model is deployed into production, it should be given the widest possible user access, so that the investment in the model is fully exploited across the firm.
cards.explanation: Widening access without regard to a model's scope is how models come to be used inappropriately. Access should follow intended use.
cards.originalText: Granting the widest possible user access, so that the investment in the model is fully exploited across the firm.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: A validated model should be frozen permanently once implemented, since any subsequent change would invalidate the completed validation.
cards.explanation: Models need periodic review, recalibration and updating as conditions change. Changes are managed through change control and re-validation, not prohibited.
cards.originalText: Freezing the model permanently once implemented, since any subsequent change would invalidate the completed validation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Ownership of a model should transfer to the technology function on go-live, since implementation is a systems matter.
cards.explanation: The model owner retains ownership, including accountability for validation and appropriate use. The technology function operates the environment but does not own the model.
cards.originalText: Transferring ownership of the model to the technology function on go-live, since implementation is a systems matter.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Best practices for model development and implementation. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Sample bias in the data used to build a model is a common error in model use and management across all industries, not only financial services.
cards.explanation: Sample bias survives a correct methodology and clean coding because everything downstream is built on an unrepresentative foundation. It is common to every industry that builds models from observed data.
cards.originalText: Sample bias in the data used to build the model

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: A strong model validation process comprises evaluation of conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring including process verification and benchmarking, and outcomes analysis including back-testing, all performed by parties independent of model development with the competence and influence to compel change, and covering vendor models as well as those built in-house.
cards.explanation: Strong validation covers conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis. It is performed by independent parties with the competence and influence to compel change, and it includes vendor models.
cards.originalText: Evaluation of conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring including process verification and benchmarking, and outcomes analysis including back-testing, all performed by parties independent of model development with the competence and influence to compel change, and covering vendor models as well as those built in-house.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: A strong model validation process consists of a single annual review of model output performed by the model's developers, who are best placed to interpret results.
cards.explanation: Model developers must not validate their own models; independence, not familiarity, is the control. Validation also covers far more than an annual review of outputs.
cards.originalText: A single annual review of model output performed by the model's developers, who are best placed to interpret results.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Outcomes analysis alone is sufficient for model validation, since a model that produces accurate forecasts is by definition sound whatever its internal construction.
cards.explanation: Outcomes analysis alone cannot tell a sound model from a lucky one, and for many models it is unavailable in any powerful form. Validation also requires evaluating conceptual soundness and ongoing monitoring.
cards.originalText: Outcomes analysis alone, since a model that produces accurate forecasts is by definition sound whatever its internal construction.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model validation should be restricted to internally built models, since vendor models carry the vendor's own validation.
cards.explanation: Vendor models are a recognised source of model risk and remain the bank's responsibility, so they fall within the scope of validation.
cards.originalText: A review restricted to internally built models, since vendor models carry the vendor's own validation.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: The use of vendor models, where proprietary methodology limits the depth of conceptual review the bank can perform, is a recognised challenge in the model validation process.
cards.explanation: Proprietary vendor methodology restricts conceptual review, so the bank must rely on benchmarking, sensitivity testing, outcomes analysis and whatever developmental evidence the vendor provides.
cards.originalText: The use of vendor models, where proprietary methodology limits the depth of conceptual review the bank can perform

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model users are required to participate in validating the models they use.
cards.explanation: Model validation must be independent of both model development and model use.
cards.originalText: The requirement that model users participate in validating the models they use

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Benchmarking a model against alternative approaches is prohibited in the model validation process.
cards.explanation: Benchmarking against alternative approaches is an expected component of both model development and model validation.
cards.originalText: The prohibition on benchmarking a model against alternative approaches

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Back-testing provides almost no discriminating power for a model whose output is a very high confidence level over a long horizon, such as a one-year economic capital measure, where the expected number of exceedances over any available history is close to zero; validation must then rest more heavily on conceptual soundness, input and parameter validation, benchmarking, and sensitivity and stress testing of the key assumptions.
cards.explanation: A back-test's power depends on the expected number of exceedances, which falls as the confidence level rises and the horizon lengthens. For one-year high-confidence models, validation leans on conceptual soundness, input validation, benchmarking and sensitivity and stress testing.
cards.originalText: A model whose output is a very high confidence level over a long horizon, such as a one-year economic capital measure, where the expected number of exceedances over any available history is close to zero; validation must then rest more heavily on conceptual soundness, input and parameter validation, benchmarking, and sensitivity and stress testing of the key assumptions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Back-testing provides almost no discriminating power for a short-horizon model with abundant observations, since a large sample makes individual exceptions statistically indistinguishable.
cards.explanation: Abundant observations increase a back-test's power, because more exceedances are expected. Back-testing loses power for high-confidence, long-horizon models such as one-year economic capital.
cards.originalText: A short-horizon model with abundant observations, since a large sample makes individual exceptions statistically indistinguishable.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Elements of validation and challenges to it. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Back-testing is an unreliable technique that has been superseded by benchmarking in supervisory model validation practice.
cards.explanation: Back-testing remains a core element of outcomes analysis wherever it has statistical power, as with daily trading VaR models.
cards.originalText: Any model, since back-testing is an unreliable technique and has been superseded by benchmarking in supervisory practice.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Role of the model risk management function. Describe, explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: The role of a model risk management function is to maintain a complete model inventory with risk tiering, own the model risk policy and methodology, perform or oversee independent validation, track findings to resolution, and report the firm's aggregate model risk against a stated tolerance to senior management and the board.
cards.explanation: Model risk is managed like other risks: the second-line function keeps a tiered inventory, owns policy and methodology, performs or oversees independent validation, tracks findings, and reports aggregate model risk against tolerance.
cards.originalText: To maintain a complete model inventory with risk tiering, own the model risk policy and methodology, perform or oversee independent validation, track findings to resolution, and report the firm's aggregate model risk against a stated tolerance to senior management and the board.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Role of the model risk management function. Describe, explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: The role of a model risk management function is to develop the firm's models centrally, so that methodology is consistent and the business is relieved of technical work.
cards.explanation: If the model risk function developed models, it would lose the independence validation depends on and become the owner of the risk it is meant to challenge.
cards.originalText: To develop the firm's models centrally, so that methodology is consistent and the business is relieved of technical work.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Role of the model risk management function. Describe, explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: The role of a model risk management function is to approve every model output before it is used in a business decision.
cards.explanation: Approving every output does not scale, becomes a formality, and puts a second-line function inside first-line decisions.
cards.originalText: To approve every model output before it is used in a business decision.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Role of the model risk management function. Describe, explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: The role of a model risk management function includes replacing internal audit's coverage of models, since specialist review is more effective than general audit.
cards.explanation: Internal audit assesses the effectiveness of the model risk management framework itself. If the model risk function replaced audit, the framework would go unaudited.
cards.originalText: To replace internal audit's coverage of models, since specialist review is more effective than general audit.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Role of the model risk management function. Describe, explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: A key challenge in designing model risk reporting is implementing the infrastructure required to deliver it, since model, finding, tier and usage data typically sit in separate systems and must be brought together before an aggregate view is possible.
cards.explanation: Aggregate model risk reporting requires joining the model inventory and tiering, validation findings, usage records and change history, which usually sit in separate systems. The obstacle is infrastructure before it is analysis.
cards.originalText: Implementing the infrastructure required to deliver the reporting, since model, finding, tier and usage data typically sit in separate systems and must be brought together before an aggregate view is possible

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Role of the model risk management function. Describe, explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Internal model risk reporting formats require supervisory approval.
cards.explanation: Internal model risk reporting formats are not subject to supervisory pre-approval, though supervisors do review the reporting.
cards.originalText: Obtaining supervisory approval for the format of internal reporting

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Role of the model risk management function. Describe, explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model risk reporting should avoid disclosing model limitations, which would undermine confidence in the framework.
cards.explanation: Model limitations must be documented and communicated to users and decision-makers, not hidden.
cards.originalText: Avoiding disclosure of model limitations, which would undermine confidence in the framework

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the three model risk case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model risk losses arise as often from correct models used in the wrong context, or from unexamined assumptions and data that were unrepresentative, as from mathematical error; and the failures typically survive because no independent party with the standing to compel change examines them.
cards.explanation: In model risk case studies the mathematics is usually defensible. Failures come from unsurfaced assumptions, unrepresentative samples or use outside intended scope, and persist because no independent party with standing examines the model and compels change.
cards.originalText: Losses arise as often from correct models used in the wrong context, or from unexamined assumptions and data that were unrepresentative, as from mathematical error; and the failures typically survived because no independent party with the standing to compel change examined them.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the three model risk case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model failures are almost always the result of coding errors, which is why implementation testing is the highest-value control.
cards.explanation: Coding errors are real but are the source most readily caught by implementation testing. Most model failures stem from unexamined assumptions, unrepresentative data or use outside intended scope.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the three model risk case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model risk is confined to complex derivative pricing models, so simple models require no governance.
cards.explanation: Model risk arises wherever a quantitative method produces an estimate used in decisions, including spreadsheets and expert-judgement scorecards.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the three model risk case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Models which have performed well historically can be relied upon without periodic review.
cards.explanation: Strong historical performance breeds unwarranted confidence. Periodic review exists because the environment drifts away from the calibration sample.
cards.originalText: The cases show that models which have performed well historically can be relied upon without periodic review.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the three model risk case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model governance should concentrate on the models with the largest historical loss experience, since past losses identify the models that matter.
cards.explanation: Error history is a backward-looking, weak predictor that under-weights models not yet stressed. Governance should be tiered by the materiality of the decisions each model supports.
cards.originalText: Concentrate governance on the models with the largest historical loss experience, since past losses identify the models that matter.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the three model risk case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Because it is impossible to determine in advance which modelling mistakes will prove catastrophic, a firm should apply proportionate but systematic controls across the whole model inventory, tiering by the materiality of the decisions each model supports rather than by the observed error history of the model itself.
cards.explanation: Many model errors are trivial and a few are catastrophic, with no reliable way to tell them apart in advance. Controls should therefore be systematic across the inventory, with intensity tiered by how much rides on each model's output.
cards.originalText: Accept that individual errors cannot be triaged reliably, and therefore apply proportionate but systematic controls across the whole model inventory, tiering by the materiality of the decisions each model supports rather than by the observed error history of the model itself.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the three model risk case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: The maximum level of validation and governance should be applied to every model in the inventory, since any error could prove catastrophic.
cards.explanation: Uniform maximum control is unaffordable, and because it must be diluted in practice, it gives critical models less protection than honest tiering by materiality.
cards.originalText: Apply the maximum level of validation and governance to every model in the inventory, since any error could prove catastrophic.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Lessons from the three model risk case studies. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 15: Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)
cards.statement: Model risk cannot be managed, so firms should rely on capital held against operational risk to absorb the consequences.
cards.explanation: Model risk is to be managed like other risk types, and holding capital is no substitute for managing it.
cards.originalText: Accept that model risk cannot be managed and rely on capital held against operational risk to absorb the consequences.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Motivations, goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The Basel Committee revised the Basel III framework in December 2017 to restore credibility in the calculation of risk-weighted assets and improve the comparability of banks' capital ratios, since excessive variability in RWAs for similar exposures across banks had undermined confidence in reported ratios.
cards.explanation: The December 2017 Basel III reforms targeted the risk-weighted denominator: excessive variability in RWAs for similar exposures had undermined confidence in reported capital ratios.
cards.originalText: To restore credibility in the calculation of risk-weighted assets and improve the comparability of banks' capital ratios, since excessive variability in RWAs for similar exposures across banks had undermined confidence in reported ratios.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Motivations, goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The Basel Committee revised the Basel III framework in December 2017 to raise minimum capital ratios materially above the levels set in the initial phase of Basel III, since those levels had proved insufficient.
cards.explanation: Raising the level of capital was an objective of the initial phase of Basel III. The December 2017 reforms targeted the credibility and comparability of risk-weighted assets.
cards.originalText: To raise minimum capital ratios materially above the levels set in the initial phase of Basel III, since those levels had proved insufficient.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Motivations, goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The Basel Committee revised the Basel III framework in December 2017 to replace the risk-weighted framework entirely with the leverage ratio, since risk weighting had been discredited.
cards.explanation: The leverage ratio complements risk-weighted requirements as a safeguard against excessive leverage, gaming and model risk; it does not replace them.
cards.originalText: To replace the risk-weighted framework entirely with the leverage ratio, since risk weighting had been discredited.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Motivations, goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The Basel Committee revised the Basel III framework in December 2017 to reduce the overall level of capital in the banking system, since the initial Basel III reforms had constrained lending.
cards.explanation: Reducing system-wide capital was not an objective of the December 2017 reforms. Their aim was to restore credibility and comparability in risk-weighted asset calculations.
cards.originalText: To reduce the overall level of capital in the banking system, since the initial Basel III reforms had constrained lending.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Motivations, goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 Basel III reforms, internal models were removed entirely across all risk types and replaced with standardised approaches.
cards.explanation: IRB approaches for credit risk survived the December 2017 reforms, subject to constraints. Internal models were removed only for operational risk and CVA risk.
cards.originalText: Internal models were removed entirely across all risk types and replaced with standardised approaches.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Motivations, goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Internal model approaches were removed for CVA risk and for operational risk, constrained for credit risk through limits on certain IRB inputs and the withdrawal of the advanced approach for some exposure classes, and backstopped across the framework by the revised output floor.
cards.explanation: The December 2017 reforms removed the AMA for operational risk and the internally modelled approach for CVA, constrained IRB through input floors and withdrawal of the advanced approach for some exposure classes, and added the revised output floor.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Motivations, goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 Basel III reforms, internal models were left unchanged, with the reforms confined to the standardised approaches.
cards.explanation: Constraining internal models was a central route of the December 2017 reforms: they were removed for operational and CVA risk, constrained for credit risk and backstopped by the output floor.
cards.originalText: Internal models were left unchanged, with the reforms confined to the standardised approaches.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Motivations, goals and impacts of the December 2017 reforms. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 Basel III reforms, internal models were extended to new risk types in order to improve risk sensitivity.
cards.explanation: The December 2017 reforms restricted internal models, removing them for operational and CVA risk and constraining them for credit risk, rather than extending them.
cards.originalText: Internal models were extended to new risk types in order to improve risk sensitivity.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Under Basel II a flat risk weight applied to all residential mortgages, whereas under the revised standardised approach to credit risk mortgage risk weights vary with the loan-to-value ratio.
cards.explanation: The loan-to-value treatment of residential mortgages is the worked example of the greater granularity and risk sensitivity in the revised standardised approach to credit risk.
cards.originalText: Under Basel II a flat risk weight applied to all residential mortgages, whereas under the revised approach mortgage risk weights vary with the loan-to-value ratio.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Under the revised standardised approach to credit risk, all corporate exposures receive a single risk weight, replacing the previous rating-dependent scale.
cards.explanation: Corporate exposures receive a more granular risk-weight look-up table under the revised standardised approach, not a single weight.
cards.originalText: Under the revised approach all corporate exposures receive a single risk weight, replacing the previous rating-dependent scale.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The revised standardised approach to credit risk increases reliance on external credit ratings, which are now mandatory in all jurisdictions.
cards.explanation: The revised standardised approach reduces mechanistic reliance on external ratings, requiring due diligence and providing a non-ratings-based approach for jurisdictions that do not use them.
cards.originalText: The revised approach increases reliance on external credit ratings, which are now mandatory in all jurisdictions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The revised standardised approach to credit risk abolishes credit conversion factors for off-balance sheet items, since these had proved unnecessary.
cards.explanation: The revised approach makes credit conversion factors more risk-sensitive and introduces a positive CCF for unconditionally cancellable commitments, which previously attracted zero.
cards.originalText: The revised approach abolishes credit conversion factors for off-balance sheet items, since these had proved unnecessary.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In the December 2017 revisions to the IRB approaches, input floors were introduced on PD and, for the advanced approach, on LGD and EAD; the foundation approach LGD for unsecured exposures to non-financial corporates was reduced from 45% to 40%; and the 1.06 scaling factor applied to IRB risk-weighted assets was removed.
cards.explanation: The December 2017 IRB revisions added input floors, cut the foundation IRB LGD for unsecured non-financial corporate exposures from 45% to 40%, and removed the 1.06 scaling factor on IRB RWAs.
cards.originalText: Input floors were introduced on PD and, for the advanced approach, on LGD and EAD; the foundation approach LGD for unsecured exposures to non-financial corporates was reduced from 45% to 40%; and the 1.06 scaling factor applied to IRB risk-weighted assets was removed.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In the December 2017 revisions to the IRB approaches, input floors were removed in order to increase risk sensitivity, and the 1.06 scaling factor was raised.
cards.explanation: The December 2017 revisions introduced input floors on IRB parameters and removed the 1.06 scaling factor rather than raising it.
cards.originalText: Input floors were removed in order to increase risk sensitivity, and the 1.06 scaling factor was raised.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In the December 2017 revisions to the IRB approaches, the foundation IRB approach was abolished, leaving only the advanced approach.
cards.explanation: The foundation IRB approach survived with recalibrated supervisory parameters. What was withdrawn was the advanced approach for certain exposure classes.
cards.originalText: The foundation IRB approach was abolished, leaving only the advanced approach.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In the December 2017 revisions to the IRB approaches, haircuts on non-financial collateral were reduced and LGD parameters increased, so that secured exposures attract higher capital than unsecured ones.
cards.explanation: The December 2017 revisions increased haircuts on non-financial collateral and reduced LGD parameters, and secured exposures do not attract more capital than unsecured ones.
cards.originalText: Haircuts on non-financial collateral were reduced and LGD parameters increased, so that secured exposures attract higher capital than unsecured ones.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The December 2017 Basel III revisions removed CVA risk from the capital framework, since it duplicates the counterparty credit risk charge.
cards.explanation: CVA risk is distinct from default risk: the counterparty credit risk charge covers default, while CVA covers mark-to-market losses from credit deterioration short of default. The CVA framework was revised, not removed.
cards.originalText: CVA risk was removed from the capital framework, since it duplicates the counterparty credit risk charge.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The December 2017 revisions to the CVA risk framework revised it to capture the exposure component of CVA risk together with its associated hedges, to strengthen robustness given the complexity of the risk, and to improve consistency with the market risk framework; the internally modelled approach was removed, leaving a standardised and a basic approach.
cards.explanation: The CVA revision aimed to enhance risk sensitivity by capturing the exposure component and its hedges, strengthen robustness given the risk's complexity, and align with the market risk framework. The internally modelled approach was removed, leaving SA-CVA and BA-CVA.
cards.originalText: The framework was revised to capture the exposure component of CVA risk together with its associated hedges, to strengthen robustness given the complexity of the risk, and to improve consistency with the market risk framework; the internally modelled approach was removed, leaving a standardised and a basic approach.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In the December 2017 revisions to the CVA risk framework, the internally modelled approach was retained and extended, since CVA is too complex for a standardised treatment.
cards.explanation: The complexity of CVA risk was a reason for removing the internally modelled approach, leaving a standardised and a basic approach.
cards.originalText: The internally modelled approach was retained and extended, since CVA is too complex for a standardised treatment.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In the December 2017 revisions to the CVA risk framework, CVA risk was reclassified as an operational risk, since it arises from the deterioration of a counterparty's creditworthiness rather than from market movements.
cards.explanation: CVA remains a market-risk-driven charge within the counterparty framework, and its treatment was aligned with the market risk framework rather than moved to operational risk.
cards.originalText: CVA risk was reclassified as an operational risk, since it arises from the deterioration of a counterparty's creditworthiness rather than from market movements.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: A single standardised approach replaces all previous approaches including the AMA; capital is the product of a Business Indicator Component and an Internal Loss Multiplier; national supervisors may set the ILM to one, in which case capital is determined solely by the BIC and is unrelated to the bank's historical losses; and all banks must disclose their historical operational risk losses even where the ILM is set to one.
cards.explanation: Operational risk capital equals the Business Indicator Component times the Internal Loss Multiplier. National supervisors may set the ILM to one, making capital depend only on the BIC, but historical loss disclosure is still required for comparability.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Under the December 2017 operational risk revisions, the AMA was retained for the largest banks, since only they hold sufficient loss data to model operational risk credibly.
cards.explanation: The AMA was withdrawn for all banks without exception; a single standardised approach applies to everyone.
cards.originalText: The AMA was retained for the largest banks, since only they hold sufficient loss data to model operational risk credibly.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Where a jurisdiction sets the ILM to one, banks in that jurisdiction are exempt from disclosing their historical operational risk losses.
cards.explanation: Disclosure of historical operational risk losses is required even where the ILM is set to one, in order to aid comparability.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The Business Indicator replaces gross income with a measure based solely on the bank's ten-year loss history.
cards.explanation: The Business Indicator is a financial-statement proxy made up of interest, lease and dividend, services and financial components. Loss history enters through the Internal Loss Multiplier, not the Business Indicator.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The leverage ratio buffer introduced by the December 2017 Basel III reforms applies to all banks, must be met with Tier 2 capital, and is set at 100% of the risk-weighted higher loss-absorbency requirement.
cards.explanation: The leverage ratio buffer applies only to G-SIBs, must be met with Tier 1 capital, and is set at 50% of the G-SIB's risk-weighted higher loss-absorbency requirement.
cards.originalText: The buffer applies to all banks, must be met with Tier 2 capital, and is set at 100% of the risk-weighted higher loss-absorbency requirement.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The leverage ratio buffer introduced by the December 2017 Basel III reforms applies to G-SIBs, must be met with Tier 1 capital, and is set at 50% of the G-SIB's risk-weighted higher loss-absorbency requirement, with capital distribution constraints imposed on a G-SIB that fails to meet it.
cards.explanation: The G-SIB leverage ratio buffer is met with Tier 1 capital and set at 50% of the risk-weighted higher loss-absorbency requirement. Falling short triggers constraints on capital distributions, mirroring the risk-weighted buffer framework.
cards.originalText: The buffer applies to G-SIBs, must be met with Tier 1 capital, and is set at 50% of the G-SIB's risk-weighted higher loss-absorbency requirement, with capital distribution constraints imposed on a G-SIB that fails to meet it.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The leverage ratio buffer introduced by the December 2017 Basel III reforms replaces the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer, so that G-SIBs are subject to a leverage-based requirement only.
cards.explanation: The leverage ratio buffer operates alongside the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer to maintain the relative incentives of both constraints; it does not replace it.
cards.originalText: The buffer replaces the risk-weighted G-SIB buffer, so that G-SIBs are subject to a leverage-based requirement only.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Summarize the revisions across five areas. Summarize
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The leverage ratio buffer introduced by the December 2017 Basel III reforms is a hard minimum rather than a buffer, so that breaching it constitutes a breach of the minimum leverage ratio requirement.
cards.explanation: As a buffer, a shortfall triggers capital distribution constraints rather than a breach of the minimum leverage ratio requirement.
cards.originalText: The buffer is a hard minimum rather than a buffer, so that breaching it constitutes a breach of the minimum leverage ratio requirement.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: The revised output floor and the approaches used. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Under the revised output floor introduced by the December 2017 reforms, a bank's risk-weighted assets must be the higher of total RWAs calculated using the approaches it has supervisory approval to use, and 72.5% of total RWAs calculated using only the standardised approaches; it replaces the Basel II floor, which was calibrated at 80% of Basel I capital requirements and had been applied inconsistently across jurisdictions.
cards.explanation: The revised output floor sets RWAs at the maximum of modelled RWAs and 72.5% of fully standardised RWAs. It replaces the Basel II floor of 80% of Basel I requirements, which had been applied inconsistently and rested on superseded standards.
cards.originalText: A bank's risk-weighted assets must be the higher of total RWAs calculated using the approaches it has supervisory approval to use, and 72.5% of total RWAs calculated using only the standardised approaches; it replaces the Basel II floor, which was calibrated at 80% of Basel I capital requirements and had been applied inconsistently across jurisdictions.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: The revised output floor and the approaches used. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: Under the revised output floor introduced by the December 2017 reforms, a bank's risk-weighted assets must be the lower of its modelled RWAs and 72.5% of its standardised RWAs, so that the floor caps the capital a modelling bank must hold.
cards.explanation: A floor takes the higher of modelled RWAs and 72.5% of standardised RWAs. Taking the lower would cap capital, the opposite of the floor's purpose.
cards.originalText: A bank's risk-weighted assets must be the lower of its modelled RWAs and 72.5% of its standardised RWAs, so that the floor caps the capital a modelling bank must hold.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: The revised output floor and the approaches used. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The revised output floor introduced by the December 2017 reforms retains the Basel I basis of the Basel II floor but recalibrates it from 80% to 72.5%.
cards.explanation: The revised output floor abandons the Basel I basis and is set at 72.5% of RWAs under the revised Basel III standardised approaches. Reliance on superseded Basel I standards was one reason the old floor failed.
cards.originalText: The revised floor retains the Basel I basis of the Basel II floor but recalibrates it from 80% to 72.5%.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: The revised output floor and the approaches used. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: The revised output floor introduced by the December 2017 reforms applies only to banks using the advanced IRB approach and has no effect on banks using the foundation approach.
cards.explanation: The output floor is an aggregate constraint on total RWAs and binds on any bank whose overall modelled RWAs fall below 72.5% of the standardised calculation.
cards.originalText: The floor applies only to banks using the advanced IRB approach and has no effect on banks using the foundation approach.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: The revised output floor and the approaches used. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In calculating the standardised leg of the output floor, a bank must use its own internal models, re-run with supervisory parameters.
cards.explanation: Internal models cannot enter the standardised leg of the output floor in any form; the floor exists to backstop modelled outcomes with standardised ones.
cards.originalText: Its own internal models, re-run with supervisory parameters

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: The revised output floor and the approaches used. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In calculating the standardised leg of the output floor, a bank must use the standardised approach for credit risk; SA-CCR for derivative exposures, with the resulting exposure amounts risk-weighted under the standardised approach for credit risk; for CVA risk, SA-CVA, BA-CVA or 100% of the bank's counterparty credit risk capital requirement depending on eligibility and use; and for securitisation, SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or a 1250% risk weight.
cards.explanation: The standardised leg of the output floor uses only the prescribed standardised approaches for each risk type, including SA-CCR exposures risk-weighted under the standardised credit risk approach and standardised CVA and securitisation methods.
cards.originalText: The standardised approach for credit risk; SA-CCR for derivative exposures, with the resulting exposure amounts risk-weighted under the standardised approach for credit risk; for CVA risk, SA-CVA, BA-CVA or 100% of the bank's counterparty credit risk capital requirement depending on eligibility and use; and for securitisation, SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or a 1250% risk weight

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: The revised output floor and the approaches used. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In calculating the standardised leg of the output floor, a bank must use the Basel I risk weights, since the floor is a backstop and should be simple.
cards.explanation: The revised output floor is based on the revised Basel III standardised approaches. Abandoning the Basel I basis was the defining change from the old floor.
cards.originalText: The Basel I risk weights, since the floor is a backstop and should be simple

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: The revised output floor and the approaches used. Describe
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
cards.statement: In calculating the standardised leg of the output floor, a bank may use whichever standardised or modelled approach produces the lower RWA figure for each exposure class.
cards.explanation: Picking the lower of standardised or modelled RWAs per exposure class would produce a floor below both alternatives, the opposite of a backstop. The floor leg uses only standardised approaches.
cards.originalText: Whichever standardised or modelled approach produces the lower RWA figure for each exposure class

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: In stress scenario design, the problem of coherence is that scenarios are inherently multi-factor, so the difficulty is not in choosing an extreme value for any one risk factor but in specifying a joint outcome across all relevant factors in which the individual movements are mutually consistent, since when one risk factor moves significantly the others move too.
cards.explanation: Stress scenarios describe adverse states of the world through several risk factors taking extreme yet coherent, meaning possible, values. When one factor moves sharply the others move too, so the joint outcome must be internally consistent.
cards.originalText: Scenarios are inherently multi-factor, so the difficulty is not in choosing an extreme value for any one risk factor but in specifying a joint outcome across all relevant factors in which the individual movements are mutually consistent, since when one risk factor moves significantly the others move too.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: In stress scenario design, coherence means selecting the single most severe historical value observed for each risk factor, so that the scenario is at least as severe as anything previously experienced.
cards.explanation: Combining the worst historical value of each risk factor independently can produce a combination that never occurred and could not occur, which is exactly the incoherence the constraint prevents.
cards.originalText: Coherence means selecting the single most severe historical value observed for each risk factor, so that the scenario is at least as severe as anything previously experienced.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: In stress scenario design, coherence requires that every risk factor move in the same direction, since a stress scenario should be uniformly adverse.
cards.explanation: Coherence does not require every factor to move adversely. Some factors, such as exchange rates or safe-haven assets, must move favourably for the scenario to be possible.
cards.originalText: Coherence requires that every risk factor move in the same direction, since a stress scenario should be uniformly adverse.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: In stress scenario design, coherence is a presentational requirement concerning the clarity of the scenario narrative rather than a modelling constraint.
cards.explanation: Coherence is a substantive constraint on the joint behaviour of risk factors in a scenario, not a matter of drafting or presentation.
cards.originalText: Coherence is a presentational requirement concerning the clarity of the scenario narrative rather than a modelling constraint.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: The coherence problem in stress scenario design is especially acute for market risk because trading books contain hundreds of thousands of positions mapped to tens of thousands of risk factors, so finding a coherent outcome in such a high dimensional space is daunting; the usual response has been to fall back on historical realisations, at the cost that a historical scenario does not test for anything new.
cards.explanation: Trading books map a huge number of positions to tens of thousands of risk factors, making coherent joint outcomes hard to specify. Firms usually fall back on historical scenarios, which are coherent by construction but cannot test for anything new.
cards.originalText: Trading books contain hundreds of thousands of positions mapped to tens of thousands of risk factors, so finding a coherent outcome in such a high dimensional space is daunting; the usual response has been to fall back on historical realisations, at the cost that a historical scenario does not test for anything new.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: Trading positions are marked to market daily, so no stress scenario is required for them at all.
cards.explanation: Daily marking to market measures current value but says nothing about value under a hypothetical stress, which is what a stress scenario is for.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: Market risk factors are independent of one another, which makes joint specification straightforward but individually severe values hard to justify.
cards.explanation: Market risk factors are strongly dependent, especially in stress, and that dependence is what makes coherent joint specification of scenarios hard.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: The coherence problem in stress scenario design is acute for market risk because trading books contain very few risk factors, so any error in specifying one has a disproportionate effect.
cards.explanation: The coherence problem in market risk comes from the very large number of risk factors in trading books, which makes coherent joint outcomes hard to find.
cards.originalText: The problem is acute because trading books contain very few risk factors, so any error in specifying one has a disproportionate effect.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: A common supervisory stress scenario ensures that results are equally severe for every participant, which is what makes cross-bank comparison meaningful.
cards.explanation: A common scenario delivers a common input, not common severity. Severity depends on how the scenario interacts with each bank's balance sheet, business mix and geographic footprint.
cards.originalText: A common scenario ensures that results are equally severe for every participant, which is what makes cross-bank comparison meaningful.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: A common supervisory stress scenario supports comparability and supervisory efficiency, but any given scenario will be more severe for some banks and much less so for others depending on business mix and geographic footprint, so a uniform scenario is not a uniform test of resilience.
cards.explanation: Imposing the same scenario on all banks aids comparability and efficiency, but its severity varies with each bank's business mix and geography. A house price collapse is severe for a mortgage lender and mild for an international corporate bank.
cards.originalText: A common scenario supports comparability and supervisory efficiency, but any given scenario will be more severe for some banks and much less so for others depending on business mix and geographic footprint, so a uniform scenario is not a uniform test of resilience.

cards.subject: Operational Risk
cards.loText: Challenges in scenario design and coherence. Explain
cards.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 17: Stress Testing Banks (Schuermann)
cards.statement: A common supervisory stress scenario removes the need for banks to run their own internal stress tests, since the supervisory scenario is by construction the most severe plausible outcome.
cards.explanation: No supervisory scenario is the most severe plausible outcome for every bank, and internal stress testing that reflects firm-specific factors is expressly expected.
